Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) -- The driver of a truck that collided with a bus in northeast Mexico, killing 12 people including 11 passengers from the United States and Canada, was intoxicated, a Mexican official said Tuesday. Emergency workers wheel a crash victim on a gurney after Monday's bus crash in Mexico. The tractor-trailer's 21-year-old driver was among those hospitalized after Monday's crash near Monterrey, Mexico, said Segismundo Doguin Martinez, a police official in the Mexican state of Coahuila. The driver of the bus was among those killed, and 15 bus passengers were injured. The Senda Express bus, operated by Grupo Senda, had been traveling from McAllen, Texas, carrying tourists to Zacatecas in central Mexico. Eight of those who died were from the United States, three were from Canada and one, the bus driver, was from Mexico, Doguin said.  Watch rescuers work at scene of deadly crash » . The survivors, most of them in grave condition, were taken to the Christus Muguerza Hospital and the Clinica La Concepcion, the Mexican official said. "They are in a delicate state but out of danger," Doguin said. El Milenio newspaper reported on its Web site that eight of the injured are from the United States, four are from Canada and three from Mexico. Seven of the injured Americans are from Texas and one is from Iowa, the newspaper said. El Norte newspaper's Web site and El Porvenir said the dead and injured included tourists. Among those killed in the crash was 73-year-old Ronald Christy, said his daughter, Pam Fordyce. Christy's wife, Margaret Christy, was in critical condition in a Mexican hospital, Fordyce said. "He was doing exactly what he loved -- traveling," Fordyce, of Altoona, Iowa, told CNN by telephone Tuesday. "He was right where he would want to be, on a bus." She said the couple wintered in Texas and lived in West Liberty, Iowa, in the summer. The U.S. consulate called her at 1:30 a.m. Tuesday to tell her that her father had been killed, Fordyce said, and then followed up with an e-mail with photographs of the crash. "I didn't even know he was on a bus," she said. "I guess I could believe [the consulate] when I talked to my brother" who knew the couple was traveling, she said. "Until then you don't want to believe anything." Doguin, the Mexican official, said the accident occurred when a truck driver went off the road and then overcorrected and swerved into oncoming traffic, hitting the bus. Video of the scene from CNN affiliate TV Azteca 13 showed the left side of the bus sheared off and the semi's cab completely flattened. Rescue efforts took five hours, TV Azteca 13 reported. The U.S. consulate in Monterrey will not release the names of the dead or injured until all family members have been notified, said consulate spokesman Todd Huizinga. "On Monday evening, staff from the consulate in Monterrey went to the Christus Muguerza Hospital to offer assistance to some of the injured who were brought there after the crash," Huizinga said. "The consulate expects to have more detail in the coming hours." The truck driver was injured and is being held by authorities at a hospital, Doguin said. The Web site for Grupo Senda says the company started in Linares, Mexico, more than 75 years ago. It provides bus service to 15 Mexican states and the Texas Valley, the site says. Elizabeth Suarez, director of the McAllen Central Bus Station, where the bus trip originated, issued a statement saying, "We are very saddened by the news this morning. We offer our condolences to the families. The city of McAllen is the landlord of the bus terminal facility in McAllen. Grupo Senda is our tenant." CNN's Melanie Whitley, Taylor Gandossy, Tess Eastment and Monica Trevino contributed to this report from Atlanta, Georgia.

outputs.L1:
MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) -- The driver of a truck that collided with a bus in northeastern Mexico, killing 12 people—including 11 passengers from the United States and Canada—was intoxicated at the time of the accident, a Mexican official reported Tuesday.

The 21-year-old driver of the tractor-trailer was among those hospitalized following Monday's crash near Monterrey, according to Segismundo Doguin Martinez, a police official in the Mexican state of Coahuila. The bus driver was also among the fatalities, and 15 bus passengers sustained injuries.

The Senda Express bus, operated by Grupo Senda, had departed from McAllen, Texas, carrying tourists bound for Zacatecas in central Mexico. Of those who perished, eight were American nationals, three were Canadian, and one—the bus driver—was Mexican, Doguin said.

The survivors, most in grave condition, were transported to Christus Muguerza Hospital and Clínica La Concepción. "They are in a delicate state but out of danger," Doguin stated.

According to El Milenio's website, eight of the injured are American, four are Canadian, and three are Mexican. The newspaper further reported that seven of the injured Americans hail from Texas, with one from Iowa. Both El Norte and El Porvenir similarly confirmed that tourists were among the dead and injured.

Among the victims was 73-year-old Ronald Christy, according to his daughter, Pam Fordyce. Christy's wife, Margaret, remained in critical condition at a Mexican hospital, Fordyce said.

"He was doing exactly what he loved—traveling," Fordyce, of Altoona, Iowa, told CNN by telephone Tuesday. "He was right where he would want to be, on a bus." She explained that the couple spent winters in Texas and summers in West Liberty, Iowa.

Fordyce recounted that the U.S. consulate contacted her at 1:30 a.m. Tuesday to inform her of her father's death, later following up with an email containing photographs from the crash site. "I didn't even know he was on a bus," she said. "I suppose I could believe the consulate once I spoke with my brother," who had known of the couple's travel plans. "Until then, you don't want to believe anything."

Doguin explained that the accident occurred when the truck driver veered off the road, then overcorrected and swerved into oncoming traffic, striking the bus. Footage from CNN affiliate TV Azteca 13 showed the bus's left side sheared away and the truck's cab completely crushed. Rescue operations lasted five hours, according to the station.

The U.S. consulate in Monterrey has withheld the names of the deceased and injured pending notification of all family members, said consulate spokesman Todd Huizinga. "On Monday evening, staff from the consulate in Monterrey went to Christus Muguerza Hospital to offer assistance to some of the injured brought there after the crash," he said. "The consulate expects to have more details in the coming hours."

The truck driver, who was also injured, remains in custody at a hospital, Doguin noted.

According to Grupo Senda's website, the company was founded in Linares, Mexico, more than 75 years ago and currently provides bus service across 15 Mexican states as well as the Texas Valley.

Elizabeth Suarez, director of the McAllen Central Bus Station—where the journey began—issued a statement expressing the company's sorrow: "We are very saddened by the news this morning. We offer our condolences to the families. The city of McAllen is the landlord of the bus terminal facility in McAllen. Grupo Senda is our tenant."

CNN's Melanie Whitley, Taylor Gandossy, Tess Eastment, and Monica Trevino contributed to this report from Atlanta, Georgia.

A tragic traffic accident near Monterrey, Mexico, has left twelve people dead after an intoxicated 21-year-old truck driver collided with a tourist bus, turning what should have been a routine journey into a scene of devastation and loss.

## The Circumstances of the Crash

According to reports, the young truck driver was found to be under the influence of alcohol at the time of the collision, a factor that authorities believe directly contributed to the deadly crash. The impact was severe enough to claim the lives of a dozen individuals, including both passengers and the bus operator himself.

## The Victims

The twelve fatalities included eleven passengers who had traveled from the United States and Canada, individuals who were likely looking forward to their journey into Mexico. Also among the deceased was the Mexican bus driver, who lost his life while transporting his passengers to their destination. This loss adds another layer of tragedy to the incident, as the driver responsible for safely guiding the tourists ultimately became one of the victims himself.

## Details of the Journey

The bus involved in the accident belonged to Senda Express, a transportation company operating a route from McAllen, Texas, to Zacatecas, Mexico. The vehicle was carrying a group of tourists on what was meant to be a cross-border journey, transporting travelers eager to explore Mexican destinations when the fatal collision occurred.

## The Injured and Their Condition

Beyond those who died, fifteen additional passengers sustained injuries in the crash and were subsequently transported to local hospitals for treatment. Medical reports indicate that most of these survivors were in grave but stable condition, suggesting that while their injuries were serious and life-threatening, they were receiving the medical care necessary to stabilize their situations in the aftermath of the collision.

## A Personal Story of Loss

Among the many personal tragedies emerging from this disaster was the story of Ronald Christy, a 73-year-old traveler from Iowa, who was among those killed in the crash. His wife, Margaret, survived the accident but suffered critical injuries that left her fighting for her life. Their story exemplifies the human dimension of this tragedy—a couple who had likely set out together to enjoy their retirement years through travel, only to have their journey ended in catastrophe. The Christys' experience serves as a poignant reminder of how such accidents can instantly and irrevocably alter the lives of ordinary travelers, particularly older adults who often use retirement as an opportunity to explore new places and create lasting memories.

This devastating collision underscores the profound risks associated with impaired driving and serves as a somber reminder of how quickly a routine trip can turn into an unimaginable tragedy for multiple families across two countries.

**OAXACA, Mexico** — A tour bus carrying approximately 40 passengers plunged off a mountainous highway in southern Mexico early Tuesday morning, killing at least 12 people and injuring more than two dozen others in one of the region's deadliest road accidents in recent years.

The bus, traveling along a winding stretch of Highway 175 that connects Oaxaca City to the Pacific coast, was carrying tourists and local residents when it veered off the road around 4:30 a.m., according to Mexican civil protection authorities. The vehicle rolled approximately 50 meters down a steep embankment before coming to rest against a cluster of trees, which authorities say may have prevented additional casualties.

## Rescue Operation Complicated by Remote Location

Emergency responders faced significant challenges reaching the crash site, located in a remote mountainous area with limited road access. Firefighters, Red Cross volunteers, and members of the National Guard worked for more than six hours to extract survivors from the wreckage, many of whom were trapped beneath twisted metal and luggage.

"The terrain made this an extremely difficult operation," said Fernando Ruiz Martínez, a coordinator with Oaxaca's Civil Protection agency. "Our teams had to rappel down the embankment carrying equipment by hand because vehicles couldn't reach the site directly. We used hydraulic tools to cut through the bus's frame to reach those who were pinned inside."

Helicopters were eventually deployed to airlift the most critically injured passengers to hospitals in Oaxaca City, while others were transported by ambulance along the narrow mountain roads. Local residents from a nearby village reportedly arrived at the scene before official rescue teams, using ropes and farming tools to begin pulling survivors from the wreckage.

## Families Await News, Grief and Uncertainty Grow

At Hospital General Dr. Aurelio Valdivieso in Oaxaca City, family members gathered anxiously throughout the day, seeking information about loved ones who had been traveling on the bus, which was en route to the coastal town of Puerto Escondido.

Maria Elena Vásquez, whose sister Carmen was among the passengers, described the agonizing wait for information.

"We heard about the accident on the news before anyone called us," Vásquez said, her voice breaking as she spoke outside the hospital. "For three hours we didn't know if she was alive or dead. When they finally told us she survived, I fell to my knees right there in the hallway. But I keep thinking about the other families who are still waiting, or who got the worst possible news. Carmen has a broken pelvis and internal injuries, but she's alive. Not everyone can say that today."

Vásquez said her sister had been traveling to visit her daughter for a family celebration. "She was so excited for this trip. Now she's in an operating room and we don't know what her life will look like after this."

The driver was among those injured and is currently unable to be questioned by investigators, according to a statement from state prosecutors.

Highway 175 has long been known among local drivers as a treacherous route, with sharp switchbacks, minimal guardrails, and few lighting fixtures for nighttime travel. Transportation safety advocates have called for stricter regulations on tour bus operators in the region, citing this as at least the third major bus accident on Oaxacan mountain highways in the past five years.

As of Tuesday evening, authorities said the death toll could still rise, as several passengers remained in critical condition. Identification of victims was ongoing, with officials working to notify families before releasing an official list of the deceased.
